method: Hand-written single-best-answer MCQs grounded only in the accepted open full text.

topic.topicDisplayName: Cardiac tamponade: Beck's triad, pericardiocentesis, surgical drainage
topic.coverageNote: ESC 2015 tamponade section. Beck's triad is not named in the text; the listed signs are used instead. A stored 2024 pericardial-imaging statement did not discuss tamponade.

mcqs.question: How does the 2015 ESC guideline define cardiac tamponade?

options.A: Life-threatening compression of the heart by pericardial fluid, pus, blood, clot, or gas
options.B: Any pericardial effusion, regardless of haemodynamic effect
options.C: Constriction of a thickened pericardium without effusion

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Life-threatening compression of the heart by pericardial fluid, pus, blood, clot, or gas
mcqs.explanation: Cardiac tamponade is life-threatening slow or rapid compression of the heart due to pericardial accumulation of fluid, pus, blood, clots, or gas.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Cardiac tamponade is a life-threatening, slow or rapid compression of the heart due to the pericardial accumulation of fluid, pus, blood, clots or gas

mcqs.question: Which clinical signs does the guideline list?

options.A: Tachycardia, hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, raised jugular venous pressure, and muffled heart sounds
options.B: Fever, splinter haemorrhages, and a new murmur
options.C: Bradycardia, hypertension, and a loud first heart sound
options.E: Only a normal examination with a large effusion on CT

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Tachycardia, hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, raised jugular venous pressure, and muffled heart sounds
mcqs.explanation: The guideline lists tachycardia, hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, raised jugular venous pressure, muffled heart sounds, low voltage with electrical alternans, and an enlarged silhouette when accumulation is slow. It does not name Beck's triad.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Clinical signs in a patient with cardiac tamponade include tachycardia, hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, raised jugular venous pressure, muffled heart sounds

mcqs.question: What is the guideline's definition of pulsus paradoxus?

options.A: An inspiratory decrease in systolic arterial pressure of more than 10 mmHg during normal breathing
options.B: A rise in systolic pressure during inspiration
options.C: Absence of the radial pulse for one minute

mcqs.correctAnswerText: An inspiratory decrease in systolic arterial pressure of more than 10 mmHg during normal breathing
mcqs.explanation: Pulsus paradoxus is conventionally an inspiratory decrease in systolic arterial pressure of more than 10 mmHg during normal breathing. The guideline calls it a key diagnostic finding.

sourceRefs.excerpt: pulsus paradoxus (conventionally defined as an inspiratory decrease in systolic arterial pressure of >10 mmHg during normal breathing)

mcqs.question: Which test does the guideline call the single most useful diagnostic tool, and what procedure does it also guide?
mcqs.explanation: Echocardiography is the single most useful diagnostic tool to identify the effusion and estimate its haemodynamic impact, and it is used to guide pericardiocentesis.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Echocardiography is the single most useful diagnostic tool to identify pericardial effusion and estimate its size, location and degree of haemodynamic impact

mcqs.question: How should tamponade be drained?

options.A: Preferably needle pericardiocentesis with echo or fluoroscopic guidance, without delay if unstable; surgery especially for purulent pericarditis or bleeding
options.B: Oral colchicine as the definitive drainage method
options.D: Pericardiectomy as the first step for every free-flowing effusion

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Preferably needle pericardiocentesis with echo or fluoroscopic guidance, without delay if unstable; surgery especially for purulent pericarditis or bleeding
mcqs.explanation: Drainage is preferably by needle pericardiocentesis with echocardiographic or fluoroscopic guidance and should not be delayed in unstable patients. Surgery is the alternative especially for purulent pericarditis or bleeding into the pericardium.

sourceRefs.excerpt: preferably by needle pericardiocentesis, with the use of echocardiographic or fluoroscopic guidance, and should be performed without delay in unstable patients. Alternatively, drainage is performed by a surgical approach, especially in some situations such as purulent pericarditis or in urgent situations with bleeding into the pericardium
